boardAlignment.summary: Physical and psychological dependence, tolerance and withdrawal in addiction.

definitionsAndCoreConcepts: Substance-use disorder involves a compulsive pattern of substance use that continues despite significant adverse consequences.
Physical dependence involves physiological adaptation such that stopping the substance can produce withdrawal symptoms.
Psychological dependence involves an emotional or motivational need for the substance, including craving or using it to relieve distress.
Tolerance occurs when increasing amounts of a substance are needed to achieve effects previously produced by lower doses.
Withdrawal is the set of adverse symptoms that can occur when use is reduced or stopped after dependence has developed.
modelsResearchAndRelationships: Tolerance and withdrawal can accompany physical dependence, while craving is particularly relevant to psychological dependence and compulsive use.
Dependence features must be interpreted within the broader pattern of impaired control and continued use despite harm rather than used as a complete definition of addiction on their own.
evaluationAndLimits: Physical dependence alone does not establish a substance-use disorder because tolerance and withdrawal can occur with medically used drugs without compulsive misuse.
misconceptionsAndBoundaries: Tolerance is not the same as withdrawal.
Psychological dependence is not imaginary; it describes motivational and emotional processes such as craving.
Dependence and addiction overlap but should not be treated as identical concepts.

boardAlignment.summary: Addiction vulnerability through genetic/biological, personality and social influences.

definitionsAndCoreConcepts: Addiction vulnerability is multifactorial: biological susceptibility, personality characteristics and social/environmental conditions can alter risk without determining outcome.
Impulsivity is a personality-related vulnerability involving poorly inhibited, rapid or reward-driven responding and is associated with substance dependence.
Novelty or sensation seeking can also correlate with substance use, but its causal status is less consistent across evidence than impulsivity.
Social influences can affect exposure, learned expectations, availability, norms and the contexts in which substance use is initiated or maintained.
modelsResearchAndRelationships: Ersche and colleagues found elevated impulsivity in unaffected siblings of stimulant-dependent participants, supporting impulsivity as a possible pre-existing vulnerability marker rather than only a consequence of drug exposure.
Contemporary reviews describe the transition toward compulsive drug use as an interaction among personality traits, social factors and neurobiological processes.
evaluationAndLimits: Risk factors are probabilistic and interactive; no single genetic, personality or social factor is sufficient to predict addiction in an individual.
Associations observed after chronic substance use can reflect consequences of use as well as pre-existing vulnerability, so temporal evidence matters.
misconceptionsAndBoundaries: A vulnerability factor is not a deterministic cause.
Personality correlates should not be interpreted as moral weakness or as fixed diagnostic labels.
Social influence is broader than direct peer pressure and includes environmental opportunity, norms and learned context.

revisionSynthesis: Revision combines independently supported biological, personality and social levels into the multifactorial course model while retaining the qualification that risk is probabilistic.

boardAlignment.summary: Nicotine addiction through neurochemical reward and learned cue reactivity.

definitionsAndCoreConcepts: Nicotine acts on neural reward systems and can increase dopaminergic signalling involved in reinforcement.
Repeated nicotine use allows environmental and internal cues to become associated with nicotine reward and withdrawal relief.
Cue reactivity occurs when learned nicotine-related cues evoke attention, craving, physiological responses or drug-seeking tendencies.
modelsResearchAndRelationships: Biological reinforcement and learned cue associations can work together: nicotine strengthens behaviour through reward-related processes while repeated pairings give surrounding cues motivational power.
Cue-induced responses help explain why craving can recur in environments previously associated with smoking even after a period of abstinence.
evaluationAndLimits: Dopamine is part of a wider neurobiological system and should not be taught as a single 'addiction chemical'.
Cue reactivity varies across people and contexts and is a risk mechanism rather than a guarantee of relapse.
misconceptionsAndBoundaries: Nicotine addiction is not explained only by conscious habit or only by dopamine; learning and neurobiology interact.
A cue can trigger craving without causing inevitable smoking behaviour.

revisionSynthesis: The interaction between neurochemical reinforcement and cue learning is Revision-authored synthesis of the separately supported mechanisms.

boardAlignment.summary: Gambling addiction through reinforcement schedules and cognitive bias.

definitionsAndCoreConcepts: Intermittent or partial reinforcement means a response is rewarded only on some occasions rather than every time.
Variable reinforcement schedules make reward timing or occurrence unpredictable and can produce persistent responding.
Gambling cognition can include systematic biases in how chance, control, near-misses, patterns and previous outcomes are interpreted.
modelsResearchAndRelationships: Unpredictable reinforcement can help maintain gambling behaviour because non-rewarded trials do not immediately signal that responding should stop.
Cognitive biases can increase the perceived value or controllability of gambling and interact with reinforcement processes to maintain repeated play.
evaluationAndLimits: Reinforcement schedules and cognitive biases are explanatory mechanisms, not complete explanations of every person's gambling disorder.
The presence of a bias does not mean a gambler is incapable of understanding probability; behaviour can reflect multiple motivational and contextual influences.
misconceptionsAndBoundaries: Variable reinforcement does not mean outcomes cease to be random in games of chance.
A run of previous outcomes does not change independent probabilities unless the game itself has a genuine dependency structure.

revisionSynthesis: Revision treats reinforcement and cognition as interacting maintenance mechanisms rather than asserting one single causal pathway.

boardAlignment.summary: Reducing addiction through medication, aversion therapy, covert sensitisation and cognitive-behavioural treatment.

definitionsAndCoreConcepts: Medication can support addiction treatment by targeting withdrawal, craving, reinforcement or other relevant biological processes, depending on the substance and treatment.
Aversion therapy applies respondent/classical-conditioning principles by pairing addiction-related cues or behaviour with an unpleasant consequence so the cue acquires an aversive response.
Covert sensitisation uses imagined aversive consequences or scenes to weaken the attractiveness of an addictive behaviour without necessarily delivering the aversive event directly.
Cognitive-behavioural therapy targets maladaptive thoughts and behaviour patterns and develops alternative interpretations, coping responses and relapse-management strategies.
modelsResearchAndRelationships: Addiction treatment commonly combines behavioural and/or psychological therapy with medication according to the individual's needs and the substance involved.
Aversion therapy and covert sensitisation both use aversive association but differ in whether the aversive event is directly experienced or represented in imagination.

A 2025 CC BY pilot study provides contemporary evidence that an aversion-based virtual-reality intervention can be studied as an adjunct to substance-use treatment, while its pilot design limits generalisation.
evaluationAndLimits: No single treatment mechanism should be assumed to work equally well across substances, people or stages of recovery.
Treatment evidence should be judged by study quality, durability of change, relapse outcomes, acceptability and safety rather than immediate response alone.
Medication supports treatment but should not be described as automatically curing the behavioural and social dimensions of addiction.
misconceptionsAndBoundaries: Aversion therapy is not the same as punishment delivered without a conditioning rationale.
Covert sensitisation is not identical to directly administered aversive conditioning because the aversive sequence is imagined.
CBT is not simply advice to stop; it systematically targets cognitions, triggers, coping behaviour and relapse risk.

definitionsAndCoreConcepts: The transtheoretical or stages-of-change model treats intentional behaviour change as a staged and potentially iterative process rather than a single event.
Precontemplation describes a stage in which there is no current intention to change the target behaviour.
Contemplation describes recognising or considering the case for change without yet taking action.
Preparation describes intending and planning to act in the near future.
Action describes active modification of the target behaviour.
Maintenance describes sustaining the changed behaviour and managing the risk of relapse.
Termination describes a state in which the target behaviour is no longer desired and temptation to return is absent or very low.
modelsResearchAndRelationships: The stages describe different readiness states and can guide the type of support that is appropriate at different points in behaviour change.
Relapse or movement between stages means the model is better understood as dynamic than as a guaranteed one-way progression.
evaluationAndLimits: The six-stage model should not be taught as a rigid ladder through which everyone progresses once and in the same order.
Termination is less commonly reached or emphasised in some applications, so maintenance and relapse management remain important practical endpoints.
misconceptionsAndBoundaries: Being aware of a problem does not by itself place someone in the action stage.
Relapse does not invalidate the model; movement backwards or renewed cycling can occur.
The stages describe readiness for change rather than guaranteeing successful behaviour change.

revisionSynthesis: The exact AQA naming is retained only as board alignment. The teaching structure is independently authored from the accepted open evidence.
